title: SpaceX Just Made Cell Towers Cool Again. Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile Are Paying the Price
detail:
SpaceX Just Made Cell Towers Cool Again. Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile Are Paying the Price
Matt Frankel, CFP®, The Motley Fool

There were some big moves in telecommunications stocks on Friday. On one hand, shares of cell tower owners Crown Castle (NYSE:CCI) and American Tower (NYSE:AMT) soared, with shares up by about 9% and 4%, respectively, as of midday. On the other hand, the three largest wireless carriers plunged, with Verizon (NYSE:VZ), AT&T (NYSE:T), and T-Mobile (NASDAQ:TMUS) all deep in the red.

Both moves are due to one company, SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX). On Thursday evening, Bloomberg reported that SpaceX is in talks to secure at least 80,000 cell sites across the United States as it aims to become the fourth nationwide wireless carrier. For context, 80,000 sites would represent about half of all the purpose-built cell towers in the U.S., so it would be a pretty big move.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

This is the second time in October that SpaceX has sent shockwaves through the telecom industry. First, on Oct. 9, SpaceX agreed to buy $8 billion in low-frequency wireless spectrum, and telecom stocks plunged. So, will SpaceX truly boost the tower companies and cost the telecom leaders money?

Why are the tower companies soaring?

First, a little context on how the cell tower business works. The owner builds a tower and then rents space on it to wireless carriers, typically under long-term leases. Next time you drive by a cell tower, take a look at the top. You'll probably see several rings of transmission equipment, and each of those represents a tenant. Since the tower is already standing, adding tenants produces extra revenue with very little additional cost.

Ever since Sprint was acquired by T-Mobile, the tower industry has essentially had three wireless customers. The majority of Crown Castle's rent comes from AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile. A well-capitalized fourth player would mean more tenants per tower.

This is also a notable expansion of SpaceX's plans. Although the company has made its telecom network ambitions known for some time, as recently as August, management described its network as small cells mounted on rooftops (not traditional towers). But without getting too technical, the low-band spectrum it bought makes large towers far more useful, so it makes sense to add them to the plan.

Of course, this isn't the first time a "fourth carrier" has emerged. Just a few years ago, Dish Network signed long-term tower leases to build its own 5G network. To make a long story short, Dish's parent company sold most of its spectrum in 2025 and began shutting down the network. Of course, SpaceX is a far more deep-pocketed tenant and could easily afford to build a nationwide network.

title: AT&T Stock Sinks on Subscriber and SpaceX Worries. Is the Stock a Buy on the Dip?
detail:
AT&T Stock Sinks on Subscriber and SpaceX Worries. Is the Stock a Buy on the Dip?
Geoffrey Seiler, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 9:43 AM MST 5 min read
T
SPCX
NVDA

AT&T (NYSE: T) stock had been on a roll, more than doubling from July 2023 to a closing high of $28.10 on March 27, 2026. However, after a strong start to 2026, AT&T stock has since come under pressure from the potential threat of Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) entering the U.S. mobile market. While the stock is becoming more attractively valued, I wouldn't be buying it just yet.

Let's dig into AT&T's recent results and prospects to see when might be a good time to buy the stock.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The SpaceX threat

AT&T CEO John Stankey addressed a potential SpaceX threat on the company's earnings call this week, although it wasn't enough to assuage investor fears. He said that low earth orbit (LEO) satellites are a way to expand wireless connectivity in rural areas, but not a means to replace wireless networks. Stankey said that in metropolitan areas, typically 40% to 45% of wireless traffic comes from inside buildings that cannot be efficiently served by traditional outdoor macro cell towers or LEOs. As such, it would take years of heavy investments for SpaceX to get to the performance levels of incumbent players.

In addition to the fears of SpaceX entering the market, investors were also not impressed with the company's wireless postpaid phone subscriber additions, which only met analyst expectations. It still added a robust 379,000 postpaid wireless phone customers in the quarter. Broadband, meanwhile, remained a bright spot. AT&T added 442,000 fiber subscribers and 327,000 fixed wireless users. It said the over 1 million advanced connectivity subscriber additions were its most in more than four years.

Turning to its results, total revenue climbed by 5.3% to $32.3 billion, while adjusted earnings per share (EPS) jumped by 20% to $0.65. The results surpassed Wall Street expectations for adjusted EPS of $0.60 on revenue of $31.7 billion.

Its advanced connectivity segment revenue increased 7.2% to $29.5 billion. Service revenue jumped 6.1% to $23.9 billion, while equipment sales rose 12.2% to $5.6 billion.

Within the segment, wireless revenue climbed 5% to $17.8 billion, while home internet revenue surged 23.4% to nearly $3 billion. Postpaid phone average revenue per subscriber (ARPU) rose 4% to $58.90, while broadband ARPU fell by 5.2% to $68.55.

Today's biggest moves

Crown Castle jumped 12% after reports that SpaceX is seeking cell tower sites for a mobile carrier service, a development that is simultaneously pressuring shares in AT&T and other mobile carriers. Meanwhile, Palo Alto Networks is climbing after Deutsche Bank named it one of three companies well-positioned to benefit from rising AI usage. What this means for investors

Artificial intelligence (AI) fears may not have receded, but it is soaring oil prices that are dominating headlines this morning. WTI crude rose 3.6% to $117 a barrel today, the highest it has been since April. Inflation concerns are weighing on markets, particularly as a further interest rate hike could happen when the Federal Reserve meet next week. As such, investor caution is likely to prevail in the near term.

Palo Alto wasn't the only cybersecurity stock to buck the trend this week. CrowdStrike and Okta also gained as markets consider potential AI-powered security threats. On Wednesday, a software vulnerability emerged that could impact 70% of websites worldwide, and that's sparked renewed analyst focus on the firms that can offer protection.

Citi sees 29%-32% valuation risk for Verizon, T-Mobile and AT&T, with another 4%-16% potential downside from current levels.

SpaceX is reportedly seeking access to at least 80,000 U.S. cell sites as it looks to establish a fourth nationwide wireless carrier.

Citi views the development as positive for Crown Castle, SBA Communications and American Tower.

Verizon Communications (VZ), T-Mobile US (TMUS) and AT&T (T) stocks came into focus Friday after Citi warned of further valuation pressure on established telecom operators as SpaceX (SPCX) advances plans to enter the U.S. wireless market.

According to a note cited by TheFly, Citi sees 29%-32% valuation risk for the three carriers, with a 4%-16% downside potential from current levels following their pullbacks in 2026.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

The firm believes SpaceX is likely to build its own telecommunications company to compete in the U.S. mobile market, rather than become a mobile virtual network operator, an outcome it considers unlikely.

At the time of writing, Verizon (VZ) shares fell more than 1%, while T-Mobile (TMUS) and AT&T (T) declined over 5% each. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment was 'bearish' for T-Mobile (TMUS) and Verizon (VZ), while AT&T (T) attracted 'bullish' sentiment.

SpaceX Eyes 80,000 Cell Sites For Nationwide Wireless Network

SpaceX is seeking access to at least 80,000 cell sites across the U.S. and is in discussions with major infrastructure providers, Bloomberg reported Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter.

The potential leasing agreements, which could be worth billions of dollars, would help SpaceX establish a fourth nationwide wireless carrier to compete with the country's dominant operators, the report said.

SpaceX has also pursued low-band wireless spectrum to complement its Starlink satellites and received Federal Communications Commission approval for 15,000 additional satellites designed to provide mobile service directly to phones.

During SpaceX's earnings call this week, CEO Elon Musk said the company plans to build terrestrial networks to provide broader connectivity wherever SpaceX and Starlink are permitted to operate.

Citi Sees Upside For Tower Operators

While Citi views SpaceX's potential entry as negative for established telecom operators, it considers the reported cell-site plans a net positive for Crown Castle (CCI), SBA Communications (SBAC) and American Tower (AMT).

Verizon (NYSE:VZ) and AT&T (NYSE:T) both raised guidance in their latest earnings reports. Retirees, however, get very different checks. Verizon offers a forward yield near 6.26% and keeps raising it. AT&T yields about 4.88% on a payout frozen since its 2022 cut. Income durability now matters more than headline yield.

NicoElNino / iStock via Getty Images
Verizon Raises the Check While AT&T Holds It Flat

Verizon raised its quarterly dividend to $0.7075 from $0.69 this year, extending a record that began at $0.565 in 2016. That steady ladder helps a retiree keep pace with inflation.

AT&T paid $0.52 per quarter until early 2022, then cut to $0.2775, where it has stayed. Management plans to hold $1.11 annualized through 2028. Predictable, yes. Yet a flat check loses purchasing power every year.

Fewer Subsidies Fund Verizon's Payout

Verizon paid $5.9 billion in first-half dividends against $10.2 billion of free cash flow, about 58% of free cash flow. The source is operational: equipment revenue fell nearly 20% as subsidies shrank, while EBITDA margin hit 40.1%. Customers still came, with 184,000 postpaid phone net adds. Management summed it up: "We're growing our dividend, and we are paying down our debt."
